The application alleged a breach of section 72(1) of the Housing Act 2004, that the respondents had control/management of an HMO within the London Borough of Camden which required an additional licence but was not licensed, and sought rent for a 12-month period beginning 13 October 2019.

The parties relied on written bundles (applicant: 101 pages plus 52-page supplementary; respondents: 72 pages) and bank statements. The occupancy agreement ran from 7 August 2019 to 7 February 2020; rent was stated as £939 pcm and the applicant was said to have remained in occupation for the claimed 12-month period.

A remote video hearing took place on 2 June 2021 before Tribunal Judge S.J. Walker and Tribunal Member A. Lewicki; the applicant was represented by counsel (Mr Sharma) and the respondents were unrepresented. The respondents raised a number of defences/mitigating points including arguments about the legal nature of the agreement (licence v assured shorthold tenancy and jurisdiction), a possible reasonable‑excuse/mitigation relating to the third respondent's health and steps said to have been taken to apply for a licence (and Covid-19 delays), claims for deductions relating to utilities/service charges and counter‑allegations about the applicant's conduct (cleaning, damage, guests, notice). A separate deposit adjudication decision appeared in the papers.

facts:
The tenant applicants applied for a Rent Repayment Order against the landlord respondent in respect of 3a John Penn Street, London SE13 7QT. The applicants named were Sofia Elvira Veliz Valencia, Christian Silva Diaz, Rocio Martinez Madrid and Linyue Kang. The accommodation comprised a self-contained flat divided into bedrooms with shared kitchen, toilet and bathroom.

The applicants relied on written agreements headed “Booking Summary” naming Simple Properties Management Ltd as the “Host”. The applicants said the documents were sham agreements and that the true tenancy arrangements involved exclusive occupation of individual rooms at stated rents: £520 pcm (Ms Madrid, total £3,170), £780 pcm (Ms Valencia and Mr Diaz, total £4,499), and £422 pcm (Ms Kang, total £1,700), paid from their earnings during stated occupancy periods.

It was alleged the Flat fell within Greenwich’s Additional Licensing Scheme and that an offence under section 72(1) of the Housing Act 2004 (control/management of an unlicensed HMO) had been committed. The applicants advanced alternative legal framing that Simple Properties acted as immediate landlord or managing agent and that the respondent was the superior leaseholder. Justice for Tenants (Mr Alasdair Mcclenehan) acted for the applicants; all applicants participated in the remote hearing on 3 March 2021 at 10 Alfred Place, London. The respondent did not file a hearing bundle and was sent directions and requests to file a statement of case.

facts:

The claimants alleged the flats were licensable HMOs under the London Borough of Hackney Additional Licensing scheme and that the landlord had not obtained the required licence.

For Flat 8 the applicants sought repayment of rent for the period 1 September 2019 to 31 August 2020 (stated claim £28,339.92). The Flat 10 applicant sought a one‑third share of rent for the period 1 August 2019 to 31 January 2020 (stated claim £4,815.30). In its documents the respondent admitted an offence under section 72(1) of the Housing Act 2004 but relied on a "reasonable excuse" defence, arguing it had relied on a managing agent and citing the ill-health of a director; the respondent also disputed the continuing tenancy status of the Flat 10 applicant and raised timing/assignment issues concerning that tenancy.

facts:
The tenant applicants (15 individual applications) brought Rent Repayment Order applications against the landlord SSG Property Developments Limited in respect of Flats 2, 3 and 4, City View@Jesmond, Eskdale Terrace, Newcastle upon Tyne NE2. Representatives were named for both parties. The Tribunal gave directions for a paper determination and both parties filed case bundles; the respondent provided a witness statement by a director dated 3 September 2019.

The tenants alleged the flats were unlicensed HMOs under section 72(1) Housing Act 2004. The tenancies were recorded as 43 weeks from 3 September 2018 at £110 per week. Licensing-related dates in the evidence included a change in licensing law effective 1 October 2018, applicants becoming aware in May 2019, licences in the bundles dated February 2019 for Flats 3 and 4, and no licence copy for Flat 2 in the bundles. Emails from a council officer gave inconsistent accounts about whether an application was attempted in October 2018 and whether an application was only recorded on 3 January 2019.

The respondent produced correspondence with HMRC about VAT treatment of the conversion works, argued that the VAT/HMRC issue affected whether an HMO licence was required, provided mitigation/financial material relating to October 2018 to January 2019, and submitted that applicants' statements were inconsistent and potentially opportunistic. Applicants relied on council advice and provided evidence of rents paid in the bundles.

The hearing was held remotely by video on 13 October 2021 at 10 Alfred Place, London; the applicants were represented by Ms Sherratt and the respondent by Ms Grewal. The respondent relied on witness statements including one from Ms Welch; some witnesses were not available for cross-examination. 

Ms Di Silvestro occupied Room 4 from 15 July 2018 to 25 March 2020, paying £550 pcm and claiming 12 months' rent of £6,600. Mr Jones occupied Room 1 from 9 March 2019 to 25 March 2020, paying £600 pcm and claiming 12 months' rent of £7,200. Both signed documents described as licence agreements (one headed as a Scottish lodger agreement) which the parties treated as tenancy agreements; the applicants alleged the wording on the deposit/rent lines showed improper handling of sums. 

There was a dispute about whether the respondent was a live-in landlord; the respondent said he occupied the property intermittently and said he had used estate-agent templates and had applied for an HMO licence with professional assistance. The respondent's evidence addressed his limited finances and significant medical history. The respondent paid utilities totalling £1,003.61 pcm (including mortgage interest) and the parties used adjusted annual rent figures of £5,665 and £6,265 for the purposes of the proceedings.

facts:
The tenant applicants applied for a rent repayment order under sections 40–44 of the Housing and Planning Act 2016 in respect of 81 Downhills Park Road, London N17. They alleged the respondent had managed an unlicensed HMO and sought £29,119.92 for the period 22 September 2019 to 21 September 2020; rent was stated as £2,426.66 per calendar month and tenancies began with an assured shorthold tenancy dated 21 September 2017, renewed annually. The applicants relied on an email from Haringey Council dated 14 April 2021 indicating no licence application had been received.

The case was heard remotely (V: CVPREMOTE) at 10 Alfred Place, London; the applicants (except one) attended with their representative Mr Alistair McClenahan and the respondent Mr Ahearne attended with solicitor Mr Richard Barca. The parties exchanged electronic bundles, skeleton arguments and other documents; HAM Estates Ltd featured as a managing agent and was removed from proceedings after representations. The respondent raised defences including a statute‑bar/6‑month prosecution argument, that some occupiers had not used the property as their principal home, possible receipt of housing element of universal credit, and a reasonable‑excuse defence based on serious ill health and shielding; he also relied on agent management and provided bank evidence and repair costs. The applicants countered that rents and council tax were paid throughout, absences were short or pandemic‑related, and that some applicants were ineligible for universal credit.
